items.prompt: What is a design pattern?
choices: A named, reusable shape for a recurring structural problem
A block of code that you must copy exactly as written in the book
A rule every well-made program has to follow
items.explanation: A pattern is a named arrangement for a recurring problem, not code to paste or a mandatory rule.

items.prompt: Strategy belongs to which family of the classic catalog?
choices: Creational, about how objects get built
Behavioral, about how objects share work
Structural, about how objects are composed together
items.explanation: Strategy swaps behavior between interchangeable objects, which is behavioral.

items.prompt: Factory Method belongs to which family?
choices: Behavioral
Structural
Creational
items.explanation: Factory Method is about how objects get built, so it is creational.

items.prompt: What does cargo-culting mean here?
choices: Copying a practice's shape without the conditions that made it work
Reusing a well-known library that many other teams already use in production
Writing code that follows a published style guide
items.explanation: Cargo-culting reproduces the visible form while skipping the reason it worked.

items.prompt: Choosing a pattern because it looks good on a CV is called what?
choices: Test-driven design
Résumé-driven design
Domain-driven design
items.explanation: The choice is driven by appearance on paper, not by what the problem needs.

items.prompt: Which is a cost that every pattern charges, whether or not it helps?
choices: Slower hardware at runtime in every case
Loss of the ability to write unit tests
More indirection and more types to read
items.explanation: Patterns add layers and types; that cost is paid even when the benefit never arrives.

items.prompt: A two-branch if/else that never changes: is a pattern needed?
choices: No, nothing there needs the flexibility a pattern buys
Yes, because any conditional should become a pattern
Yes, because patterns are always faster than if/else
items.explanation: No variation pressure means no problem for the pattern to solve.

items.prompt: What is an axis of variation?
choices: Any line of code that contains an if statement
Where behavior really differs and keeps on changing
The number of files inside a project folder
items.explanation: It is the real, repeated difference a pattern is meant to isolate, like which processor or region.

items.prompt: A teammate says 'every function with an if should use a pattern, that is best practice.' What is the weakness in that claim?
choices: Nearly all code has conditionals, so it cannot single out code needing a pattern
It is correct for functions above a certain number of lines, so only small ones are exempt
Patterns apply only to loops, so conditional logic is the wrong place to look
It would force every conditional to use inheritance instead of interfaces and composition
items.explanation: A test that nearly all code passes cannot select anything. The deciding evidence is real variation, not the presence of an if.
items.reference:
A pattern is a tool, not a badge
named shape for a recurring problem
cargo-cult: copy the shape, skip the reason
cost always paid: more types, more indirection
benefit only when the flexibility is used
Why: a pattern pays off only where its problem actually exists.
items.learnMore:
Pattern as vocabulary

A pattern name is shorthand for a problem plus an arrangement of types that solves it. It is useful in conversation and harmful as a checklist item to tick for its own sake.

Common mistake

Treating pattern use as proof of quality. The code is judged by whether it fixes a real problem, not by the names in it.
items.reflection: Think of a tool or method you adopted because it looked professional. What problem was it supposed to solve, and did you actually have that problem?

items.prompt: A change turns a 6-line function into 1 interface, 2 classes and 1 factory with identical behavior and no planned growth. What is the best description?
choices: A neutral refactor, since behavior is unchanged and tests still pass without edits
All the costs of the pattern were paid and none of its benefits were collected
An improvement in testability, because classes are always easier to test than functions
A performance gain, because virtual dispatch is cheaper than evaluating a branch
items.explanation: Same behavior plus more types and indirection with no new capability is pure cost. Unchanged tests show nothing was gained.

items.prompt: Which situation is cargo-culting rather than sound pattern use?
choices: Adding a registry so five teams can add processors without editing shared code
Wrapping a service with logging because several services need the same logging
Adding a factory that only calls the constructor, because a framework example had one
Using a lookup table because three regions differ only by a number
items.explanation: Only the first copies the shape (a factory) without the reason (complex construction used in many places).

items.prompt: Why can a pattern's name help even when the code is not changed?
choices: It guarantees the code behind that name has been reviewed for correctness already
It makes the compiler optimize the named arrangement better than plain code
It removes the need to explain why the arrangement was chosen at all
It lets two people agree on a whole arrangement of types in one word
items.explanation: The value of the name is shared vocabulary. It guarantees nothing about quality or about whether the pattern fits.

items.prompt: Q1 asks about variants. Which ones count?
choices: Real ones that exist in the code today
Ones the team imagines needing someday
Ones another company is known to have
items.explanation: A pattern built for hypothetical variants is a bet, not a fix.

items.prompt: What does Q2 check?
choices: Whether the code uses more than one programming language in total
Whether variants change independently of the surrounding code
Whether the variants share the same function name
items.explanation: Without independent change there is no seam to isolate.

items.prompt: What does Q3 check?
choices: Whether the direct version was written by the same person
Whether the direct version has comments on every line
Whether the direct version is already costing something
items.explanation: A short, stable if/else has nothing to repay.

items.prompt: What does Q4 check?
choices: Whether the indirection buys something concrete
Whether the pattern has a famous name in the catalog
Whether the indirection adds at least one extra class
items.explanation: If the same logic is just spread across more files, nothing concrete was bought.

items.prompt: Most answers are 'no'. What should you do?
choices: Apply the pattern anyway to be safe
Keep the plain version
Delay the decision to a later release by splitting the file
items.explanation: Mostly no means the direct version is right-sized.

items.prompt: Which is a real benefit that can answer Q4 with yes?
choices: Making the file longer so it looks more thorough
Using more advanced vocabulary in the codebase
Adding a new case without editing existing code
items.explanation: Extension without editing old code is a concrete gain.

items.prompt: Two branches were added in one change and never differ afterward. Which question fails?
choices: Q2, they do not vary independently
Q1, there are fewer than two branches
Q4, interfaces cannot be used for branches
items.explanation: Two real variants exist (Q1 passes), but they change together.

items.prompt: Why is 'it might need to grow later' a weak reason?
choices: Code never grows after the first release ships
It is a guess; Q1 asks for variants existing today
Later changes cannot be made without a pattern at all
items.explanation: A hypothetical future is a bet. The test reads the code as it is now.

items.prompt: Three tax rules exist today, but all three were written together and are only ever changed together in one release. Which question most clearly says to skip the pattern?
choices: Q2: nothing varies independently, so there is no seam worth isolating
Q1: three rules is below the minimum number of variants the test requires
Q4: patterns cannot be used when more than two rules are present
Q3: any code with three branches is automatically cheap to maintain
items.explanation: Q1 passes with three real variants. The failure is Q2: variants that always change together give a pattern nothing to separate.
items.reference:
Four questions before a pattern
Q1: 2+ real variants today?
Q2: variants change independently?
Q3: direct version already costly?
Q4: indirection buys something concrete?
Why: mostly yes means use the pattern, mostly no means write it directly.
items.learnMore:
Why four questions

Each question removes a different false reason: imagined variants (Q1), changes that always travel together (Q2), a cheap stable version (Q3), and abstraction that only spreads the same logic over more files (Q4).

Common mistake

Answering Q1 yes and stopping. Two variants that change together and cost nothing still fail the test.
items.reflection: Pick a process or tool you use that has a handful of steps. Which of the four questions would it fail, and what would have to change for it to pass?

items.prompt: A 40-line chain is edited by five teams and conflicts every sprint (assumed). Which question does that fact answer, and how?
choices: Q1: it proves a sixth variant is certain to arrive soon
Q3: the direct version is already causing real cost
Q4: it proves the indirection will be free to maintain
Q2: it proves the variants are written in the same language
items.explanation: Repeated conflicts and growth are evidence that the direct version is costing something now, which is exactly Q3.

Q4: indirection buys something concrete?
Why: mostly yes means use the pattern, mostly no means write it directly.

items.prompt: After a region count grows from 2 to 6 owned by different teams, the verdict flips. What does that show about the test?
choices: It was wrong the first time and should never have been applied to small code
Patterns become correct automatically once a file passes a line count
It reads the code's current shape, so it must be re-run when the shape changes
A verdict is permanent once written in a review comment or design note
items.explanation: The verdict follows the evidence. New independent owners change Q2 and Q3, so the answer changes.

items.prompt: Which pattern swaps among interchangeable algorithms at runtime?
choices: Singleton
Observer
Strategy
items.explanation: Strategy puts each algorithm behind one interface so they can be exchanged.

items.prompt: Which pattern notifies a changing set of listeners?
choices: Observer
Decorator
Factory Method
items.explanation: Observer lets a source announce events without knowing who listens.

items.prompt: Which pattern adds combinable behaviors without a subclass per mix?
choices: Singleton
Decorator
Strategy
items.explanation: Wrappers stack in different combinations, so no class per combination is needed.

items.prompt: Which pattern guarantees exactly one shared instance?
choices: Factory Method
Observer
Singleton
items.explanation: Singleton limits a type to one instance.

items.prompt: Which pattern centralizes non-trivial object construction?
choices: Factory Method
Decorator wrapper
Strategy swap
items.explanation: It moves varying construction logic into one place.

items.prompt: A factory that only calls `new Foo()` is a sign of what?
choices: Correct use, since every constructor needs a factory
Cargo-culting: one line hidden behind ceremony
A performance optimization of object creation
items.explanation: A factory earns its place when construction is complex and reused.

items.prompt: Observer with exactly one hardcoded listener: what is simpler?
choices: Adding a second listener that does nothing
Replacing the event with a global variable
Calling that one listener directly with no events
items.explanation: With one fixed listener, there is no changing set to notify.

items.prompt: What is the usual cost of Singleton?
choices: Global state and hidden dependencies in callers
An extra wrapper class for every method
A new interface for each variant in use
items.explanation: Shared global state makes dependencies invisible and tests harder.

items.prompt: Logging, retry and caching must combine in different mixes across eight services. Which pattern matches that problem?
choices: Singleton, because there is only one logging concern in the whole system
Factory Method, because services must be created in a central place
Observer, because each service has to broadcast its own retries to listeners
Decorator, because each behavior wraps the same interface and they stack freely
items.explanation: Combinable responsibilities without a class per mix is the problem Decorator was named for.
items.reference:
What common patterns solve
Strategy: swap among interchangeable algorithms
Factory Method: centralize varying construction
Decorator: combine behaviors without a class per mix
Observer: notify a changing set of listeners
Singleton: exactly one shared instance
Why: each name stands for one problem; use it only where that problem is real.
items.learnMore:
Match the problem, then the name

Start from the problem you can describe in plain words. Only then ask which named shape fits. If you cannot state the problem without the pattern's name, you probably do not have it yet.

Common mistake

Picking by familiarity. Singleton in particular is often chosen for convenient global access, which a passed-in dependency does with less hidden state.
items.reflection: Think of a kitchen, a workshop or a team you know. Where does one of these five problems (swap, build, combine, notify, share one) already exist without anyone naming it?

items.prompt: A reviewer proposes Singleton for a config object only because it is convenient to reach from anywhere. What is the strongest objection?
choices: Convenience is no real one-instance need; pass it in instead
Config objects are always larger than a single instance can safely hold in memory
Singleton cannot be used for read-only data, so it would not compile
Singleton forces every caller to be written in the same module as the config
items.explanation: The pattern's problem is a true limit of one instance. Convenient access alone is a dependency-hiding cost, not a reason.

items.prompt: Which pair correctly matches pattern to its cargo-cult sign?
choices: Strategy with five growing variants chosen at runtime by configuration
Observer with a single hardcoded listener, where a direct call would do
Decorator with several behaviors combined in different mixes per service
Factory Method with complex construction reused at many call sites
items.explanation: Three options are the 'good sign' column. Only the single listener is the cargo-cult sign.

items.prompt: Which statement about the cost side of the catalog is accurate?
choices: Only creational patterns add cost, since the other two families add almost none
The cost disappears once a team has used the pattern in three projects
Every pattern charges indirection, and repays it only when its problem exists
Cost matters for large systems only, so small code can ignore it
items.explanation: Indirection is paid by every pattern at every size; only the problem repays it.

items.prompt: Two regions differ only by a number. What is the right-sized solution?
choices: An interface with two classes and a factory
A registry that other teams add classes into
A plain lookup table keyed by region name
items.explanation: Data-only differences need data only.

items.prompt: Adding a third region to a lookup table takes how much code?
choices: One line
A new interface and a new factory
A rewrite of the existing two regions
items.explanation: Adding to a table is one entry.

items.prompt: A region now needs different calculation logic. What fits first?
choices: A full class hierarchy with abstract methods
A lookup of functions with one per region
A global singleton that holds every region
items.explanation: Functions are values, so a map of functions swaps logic with little ceremony.

items.prompt: When does class-based Strategy beat a map of functions?
choices: When any variant has more than two lines of code in it
When the calculation is slightly harder than before
When variants need state, setup or injected collaborators
items.explanation: Lifecycle and state are what closures hold poorly.

items.prompt: The direct version is 'less extensible'. Is that fair here?
choices: No, it is exactly as extensible as the problem needs
Yes, because all direct code is always hard to extend
Yes, because tables cannot be edited after they are written
items.explanation: Extensibility beyond current need is unpurchased flexibility.

items.prompt: Over-applied Strategy for two branches adds how many new types?
choices: Zero, it only renames the function and nothing else
Four: one interface, two classes and one factory
Twelve, one for each line of the original function
items.explanation: That is the cost shown in the unit's example.

items.prompt: A reader wants the international shipping cost. Which version is quicker to read?
choices: The Strategy version, spread across four definitions
Both are identical in how much must be read
The lookup, where the value sits on one line
items.explanation: Direct code keeps the behavior in one visible place.

items.prompt: Is a harder calculation by itself a reason for Strategy?
choices: No, it is not one of the four questions
Yes, any hard calculation needs an interface
Yes, harder code is always more testable as a class
items.explanation: Complexity alone does not show independent variation or cost.

items.prompt: International shipping needs weight-based pricing while domestic stays flat, all in one team's code. What is the most proportionate change?
choices: Introduce a factory and one class per region, since logic now differs
Keep numbers only and add weight handling inside the checkout function
Move the table into a global singleton so every module can edit it
Replace the number table with a table of functions keyed by region
items.explanation: Logic now differs, but nothing else does: no state, no independent owners. A table of functions covers that cheaply.
items.reference:
Escalate only as far as the problem needs
numbers differ: lookup table
logic differs: table of functions
state or lifecycle differs: class-based Strategy
Why: each step adds cost, so take the smallest one that fits.
items.learnMore:
The ladder before the pattern

Functions are values, so a map of functions already swaps behavior by key. Class-based Strategy becomes the better tool when each variant carries state, setup or injected collaborators.

Common mistake

Jumping straight to the top of the ladder because the middle one 'does not look like a pattern'.
items.reflection: Where have you reached for a heavier tool than the job needed? What would the smallest tool that still worked have been?

items.prompt: Each region's calculator must hold a live connection to a rate service and be created with injected clients. What changes?
choices: Variants now carry state and setup, so class-based Strategy begins to pay off
Nothing, because a table of functions can hold open connections just as cleanly
A lookup of numbers is still enough, since the values are all numbers
The pattern is now forbidden, because state makes patterns unsafe
items.explanation: State and lifecycle are the reason closures stop being a comfortable home. The ladder's next rung is justified by that, not by effort or taste.

logic differs: table of functions
state or lifecycle differs: class-based Strategy
Why: each step adds cost, so take the smallest one that fits.

items.prompt: A reviewer says the lookup table is 'not extensible'. How should that be assessed?
choices: Accept it, since plain tables cannot grow in any way after they are first written
Ask what extension is expected, since a table already adds regions in one line
Accept it, since extensibility always outweighs the reading cost of extra layers
Reject it, since extensibility is never a valid concern during any code review
items.explanation: The claim is only meaningful against a specific expected change. Here the expected change is cheap to make.

items.prompt: How many processors are live in the payment example?
choices: Two
Five
Nine
items.explanation: Card, wallet, bank transfer, crypto and buy-now-pay-later.

items.prompt: Why did Strategy fit payments but not shipping?
choices: Payments is written in a different language
Shipping code is always too short for any pattern
Payments had separate owners and costly shared code
items.explanation: Q2 and Q3 passed for payments and failed for shipping.

items.prompt: What lets a team add a processor without editing shared code?
choices: A registry that each team adds one line to
A longer if/else chain in the checkout function
A copy of the checkout function for each team
items.explanation: Registration moves the change into the team's own code.

items.prompt: What does Decorator avoid in the payments example?
choices: Having any logging code in the checkout flow at all
A class for every combination of retry and logging
Calling the processor more than once per charge
items.explanation: Wrappers stack, so combinations are assembled instead of written out.

items.prompt: Which processor should not auto-retry a failed charge?
choices: The card processor
The bank transfer processor
The crypto gateway
items.explanation: The example's rule: card and bank retry, crypto does not.

items.prompt: With Decorator, how is retry-plus-logging built?
choices: By wrapping one behavior inside the other one
By copying both into a new subclass for each mix
By adding a retry flag to every processor
items.explanation: Each decorator wraps an inner object of the same interface.

items.prompt: Which question does 'the shared chain is the most conflict-prone function' answer?
choices: Q1, how many variants exist in the system today
Q3, the direct version is already costing them
Q4, whether tests can run without any network
items.explanation: Repeated conflicts are present cost.

items.prompt: Why is the crypto team's separate schedule relevant?
choices: It proves crypto is the fastest of the processors
It means that crypto code needs no tests at all
It shows variants change independently (Q2)
items.explanation: Different timelines are evidence of independent variation.

items.prompt: Every payment processor ends up wrapped in exactly the same Retry-then-Log stack. What does that do to the case for Decorator?
choices: It strengthens it, because a uniform stack is easier for readers to scan
It has no effect, since Decorator is justified by the number of wrappers alone
It weakens it, because the behaviors no longer combine in different mixes
It proves that Strategy must also be removed from the payments code
items.explanation: Decorator's problem is varied combinations. A fixed identical stack can be a plain function or one class.
items.reference:
Payment processing passes all four
Q1: 5 variants live
Q2: separate teams, separate schedules
Q3: shared chain keeps conflicting
Q4: each processor tested alone
Why: the registry lets a team add a variant without editing shared code.
items.learnMore:
Why the registry, not the interface, earns Strategy

The interface alone is ceremony. The gain is that a new variant registers itself in its own change, so teams stop editing the same function. Decorator is earned the same way: the behaviors really combine in different mixes.

Common mistake

Judging by code shape. The same interface that was waste for two branches is justified here because the evidence changed, not the syntax.
items.reflection: Think of a shared document or shared checklist several people edit. What would change if each person owned a separate piece that plugged in?

items.prompt: Checkout still has one 40-line chain (assumed), but all five processors are owned by one team that ships them together. Which question now fails most clearly?
choices: Q1: five variants are still not enough to count as real
Q4: registries can never allow adding a case safely
Q3: a chain that long can never cost anything to edit
Q2: the variants do not change independently of each other
items.explanation: Five real variants exist, but one team changing them together removes the separate-owner pressure that made the registry pay.
items.reference:
Payment processing passes all four
Q1: 5 variants live
Q2: separate teams, separate schedules
Q3: shared chain keeps conflicting
Q4: each processor tested alone
Why: the registry lets a team add a variant without editing shared code.

The interface alone is ceremony. The gain is that a new variant registers itself in its own change, so teams stop editing the same function. Decorator is earned the same way: the behaviors really combine in different mixes.

Common mistake

Judging by code shape. The same interface that was waste for two branches is justified here because the evidence changed, not the syntax.
items.reflection: Think of a shared document or shared checklist several people edit. What would change if each person owned a separate piece that plugged in?

items.prompt: Which evidence best supports adopting Strategy for payments, as opposed to merely wanting it?
choices: Repeated edit conflicts in one function, plus separate owners and test needs
A reviewer's comment saying the function looks old-fashioned and ought to change
A blog post listing Strategy as a recommended pattern for every team to use
The fact that five is more than the number of branches in the shipping example
items.explanation: Evidence from the code and the teams, not opinion or catalog popularity, answers the four questions.

Q1: 5 variants live
Q2: separate teams, separate schedules
Q3: shared chain keeps conflicting
Q4: each processor tested alone
Why: the registry lets a team add a variant without editing shared code.
items.learnMore:
Why the registry, not the interface, earns Strategy

The interface alone is ceremony. The gain is that a new variant registers itself in its own change, so teams stop editing the same function. Decorator is earned the same way: the behaviors really combine in different mixes.

Common mistake

Judging by code shape. The same interface that was waste for two branches is justified here because the evidence changed, not the syntax.
items.reflection: Think of a shared document or shared checklist several people edit. What would change if each person owned a separate piece that plugged in?

items.prompt: A pattern was right at adoption. Is it right forever?
choices: No, the evidence behind it can change
Yes, a correct choice stays correct
Yes, once a review has approved it
items.explanation: The test reads current shape, so it can flip.

items.prompt: Payments drop permanently to 2 processors. What has happened to the registry?
choices: It has become more valuable to the team now
It has turned into the over-applied case
It has become impossible to remove at all
items.explanation: Two stable variants no longer pass Q2 and Q3.

items.prompt: Which wrapper order logs once per charge however many retries happen?
choices: Retry outside Log
Neither order does
Log outside Retry
items.explanation: The outer logger sees only the final outcome.

items.prompt: Which wrapper order logs each attempt separately?
choices: Retry outside Log
Log outside Retry
Both orders do
items.explanation: Each retry passes through the inner logger.

items.prompt: Where should intended wrapper order be recorded?
choices: Only in a hallway conversation
Where the wrappers are assembled
Nowhere, the compiler enforces it
items.explanation: A comment at the composition site keeps the choice visible.

items.prompt: An interface built for variants that do not exist yet fails which question?
choices: Q3, the code in question is too short to matter
Q4, interfaces are never allowed in such code
Q1, there are not two real variants to find
items.explanation: Imagined variants do not count.

items.prompt: Wrapping logic only to avoid touching another team's file is what?
choices: A misuse, as the behavior is not really independent
A good use, since it avoids merge conflicts for them
The textbook definition of the Decorator pattern
items.explanation: Avoidance is not independent variation.

items.prompt: What is the realistic way to remove an outlived pattern?
choices: Delete every file in one large and risky release
Collapse it during the next substantial change
Never touch it again under any circumstances at all
items.explanation: A migration has cost; piggyback on work already planned.

items.prompt: Payments consolidate permanently from 5 to 2 processors. What is the best next step?
choices: Delete the interface this week, since two cases never need one at all in practice
Stop planning for new processors; collapse it during the next big change there
Keep it untouched forever, since removing a pattern is always a regression
Add three placeholder processors so the registry keeps its original purpose
items.explanation: The verdict has changed but a migration has its own cost. Folding the cleanup into planned work balances both.
items.reference:
Patterns need re-checking
adopted correctly: 5 processors
later: 2 stable processors
same code is now the over-applied case
wrapper order changes what is logged
Why: the verdict is a snapshot, so re-ask the questions as the code changes.
items.learnMore:
Snapshots and written decisions

Evidence changes: owners merge, variants retire. Re-run the questions when touching long-lived pattern code, and write down choices that cannot be seen from the code, like wrapper order.

Common mistake

Removing the pattern in a big dedicated project. Collapse it the next time the area needs substantial change anyway.
items.reflection: Think of a rule or process your team adopted for good reasons that may no longer apply. What evidence would tell you it has outlived its reason?

items.prompt: A charge fails twice, then succeeds on the third attempt. With Retry outside Log, how many log lines does the charge produce, ignoring other logging?
choices: One, for the final success
Two, one per failure
Three, one per attempt
Zero, since failures are never logged
items.explanation: Retry calls the logged inner object each time, so every attempt is logged.

items.prompt: A team wraps an unrelated check in a Decorator mainly to avoid editing a file owned by another team. What is the honest assessment?
choices: It passes Q2, since two teams are now involved in the change
It passes Q4, since any new wrapper counts as concrete benefit
It is irrelevant, since patterns are never judged by motive
It fails Q2: this is avoidance, not independent behavior
items.explanation: Q2 asks whether behavior varies independently, not whether someone prefers to avoid a shared file.

items.prompt: Why is 'adopted correctly once' not enough to leave a pattern alone?
choices: Variants, owners and costs change, so an old yes can silently become a no
Patterns are guaranteed to degrade after a fixed number of months
Reviewers may reverse any approved decision without new evidence
Compilers deprecate patterns that have not been modified for a year
items.explanation: The questions are about the current shape of the code, which drifts.
